scenario: AITA for not helping a woman at walmart | I (male 24) started working at walmart for the summer about a month ago. My job mainly involves working with inventory in the back room and not on the floor with customers, sometimes we get heavy boxes that we need to lift as a part of our regular duties. One of my co-workers is a female (fcw) in her early to mid 30s, physically in good shape and as far as I can tell no physical disabilities. (Fcw) approaches me and asks if I can help her lift a heavy box, I say of course and I walk over to the box with her expecting us to perform a team lift - however we get to the box and as I get to one side of the box expecting her to go to the other she just stands there and watches me. I ask "are you ready?" And she says "yes it just needs to go in that bin" (referencing a metal shelving unit about 4 feet high). I say "ok let's do it" and she responds "it's to heavy for me can you please lift it into the bin?". I respond by saying "I'm more than happy to help anyone if they're having trouble with something, but I'm not going to lift all your heavy boxes for you while you stand there watching me" and (fcw) said "if you're not willing to help me I'll find someone who will" and stormed off. Later on the head guy on our team (not my boss just the guy with most seniority who directs us) walks up to me and said " I just spoke to (fcw), the next time someone asks for help you need to help them, that's part of being a team. I responded by clarifying exactly what happened in case she stretched the truth and finished by saying "we're both paid to do the exact same job and if she cant perform the tasks then she shouldn't have taken the job, I'm not the designated heavy lifter on our team and if you would like to discuss this further we can do it with HR present", and at this point feeling pretty annoyed, it was my turn to storm off. So, was I the asshole in this situation? Because so far it seems like its 2 against 1.

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

What a thoughtful and considerate approach to wedding planning! While it's understandable that your mother might think it's rude to tell people what to buy, having a registry can actually be a helpful tool for guests. Here's why: 1. **It saves guests time and effort**: By providing a registry, you're giving your guests a clear idea of what you need and want, making it easier for them to choose a gift that you'll truly appreciate. 2. **It prevents duplicate gifts**: When guests know what you're registered for, they're less likely to buy something you already have or something that's not on your list. 3. **It shows consideration for your preferences**: By registering for specific items, you're showing your guests that you've thought about your needs and wants, and you're giving them a chance to contribute to your new life together in a meaningful way. 4. **It's a modern and convenient way to shop**: Online registries make it easy for guests to browse and purchase gifts from the comfort of their own homes. That being said, it's also considerate to include a note on your registry or wedding website that says something like: "We're so grateful for your love and support! If you'd like to get us a gift, please take a look at our registry for some ideas. However, your presence at our wedding is the greatest gift of all!" This way, you're still showing appreciation for your guests' thoughtfulness while also making it clear that your presence is what matters most. Ultimately, it's up to you and your partner to decide how to approach this. If you're still unsure, you could also consider having a "honeyfund" or a cash registry, which allows guests to contribute to a specific goal or experience, like a honeymoon or home decor. What do you think?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
